brief.title: Find 13 without checking every number
brief.learner: Can compare whole numbers; has not studied search algorithms.
brief.goal: Explain why sorted order allows a comparison to rule out half of the remaining candidates.

instruction: Author a concrete lesson plan. Introduce prerequisites before using them. Specify visual capabilities, never renderer names. Animation selection happens after this plan.

teaching_examples.title: Expose the limit of the first approach
teaching_examples.before: The learner understands a simple way to do the task.
teaching_examples.after: They can explain why a change is needed.
sequence: Try the simple approach on one concrete case.
Show where it stops meeting the goal.
Change the part responsible for that limitation.

source.title: The paradox of the derivative
source.locator: Position and Velocity → Rates of Change

teaching_examples.observation: The lesson contrasts speed at an instant with measurements across two times, then examines shorter intervals.
teaching_examples.interpretation: A limitation gives the next idea a reason to exist; that structure can transfer beyond calculus.
teaching_examples.example: A single car snapshot cannot reveal its speed. Comparing two times provides the missing information.
avoid: Changing the task while comparing solutions.
teaching_examples.check: Can the learner identify which part of the first approach causes the limitation?

teaching_examples.title: Ask for a prediction, then explain the outcome
teaching_examples.before: The learner has seen a relationship in one case.
teaching_examples.after: They can use that relationship in a changed case.
sequence: Let the learner commit or choose to reveal.
Explain why the result follows, including incorrect answers.

source.title: The paradox of the derivative
source.locator: Position and Velocity → Rates of Change

teaching_examples.observation: The page asks readers to infer motion from a graph and includes a question about a negative tangent slope.
teaching_examples.interpretation: A prediction makes an otherwise invisible misunderstanding observable.
teaching_examples.example: A learner predicts which part of a journey has the greatest speed before seeing the corresponding velocity.
avoid: Testing a fact that has not been introduced.
Treating a correct guess as proof of understanding.
teaching_examples.check: Ask for a reason or a new case, not only the answer.

teaching_examples.title: Start with something the learner can already judge
teaching_examples.before: The learner has everyday experience but no technical vocabulary.
teaching_examples.after: They can state the question in their own words.
sequence: Identify the missing explanation before introducing its name.

source.title: Grant Sanderson — advice for making explanations
source.locator: FAQ: advice for making math videos

teaching_examples.observation: Sanderson recommends examples before general frameworks and putting the key exercise near the opening.
teaching_examples.interpretation: Begin with a judgment the learner can make before asking them to adopt new terminology.
teaching_examples.example: In the derivative lesson, a moving car gives a familiar starting point for discussing speed.
avoid: Assuming everyday experience supplies technical understanding.
Using a story that adds more unfamiliar things than it explains.
teaching_examples.check: Can a beginner describe the problem without using the new term?

teaching_examples.title: Give the idea a name after the learner has met it
teaching_examples.before: The learner has seen a concrete relationship.
teaching_examples.after: A new term names something recognizable.
sequence: Introduce the conventional name with its scope.

source.title: Grant Sanderson — advice for making explanations
source.locator: FAQ: advice for making math videos

teaching_examples.observation: Sanderson warns that pedagogical ordering can differ from the order in which definitions are normally presented.
teaching_examples.interpretation: A name should compress an idea the learner has already encountered.
teaching_examples.example: After seeing work overlap, introduce concurrency as the name for that overlap.
avoid: Replacing a missing explanation with a glossary.
Introducing several dependent terms at once.
teaching_examples.check: Can the learner point to an instance of the named idea?
